script.title: Teens and summer money: money flips, free game coins and check-first babysitting jobs
script.hook: 3 scams go after teens every summer, right when they first have money of their own. Here's each one, and the talk that stops all three.

segments.heading: Why summer
segments.narration: Summer is when a lot of teens get their first real money: a job, babysitting, birthday cash in a payment app. Scammers know it. The three scams in this video all show up in a teen's feed or messages, and all three rely on the same thing, a teen who hasn't seen the trick before. So let's show them the trick.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Money flips
segments.narration: Scam one is the money flip. A post says send fifty dollars and get five hundred back, with fake screenshots of happy customers. Nobody can multiply money you send them. Once the fifty is sent, it's gone, and then comes a release fee, then a verification fee, then a tax. Cash App itself warns about this. The rule is simple: payment apps are for people you know in real life.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Free game coins
segments.narration: Scam two is free game currency. A video or a site promises unlimited free coins, just log in. There's no generator. The site keeps the username and password, and the scammer takes the account, the items and anything bought with real money. Roblox says it plainly: free Robux generators are scams. The rule: the password goes into the game, and nowhere else.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check-first jobs
segments.narration: Scam three is the job that pays before it starts. A family hires your teen to babysit by text, mails a check for more than the pay, and asks them to send the extra to a supplier. The bank shows the money, then the check bounces days later, and your teen owes the bank everything they sent. The FTC has warned about this one again this year. The rule: no real job pays you first and asks for money back.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Settings
segments.narration: Now the settings. On screen, I'm going through my own payment app and game account. Turn on two-step verification on both. Set payments to private so strangers can't see who your teen pays. Turn on payment notifications. And on game accounts for younger kids, set a parent PIN so purchases and settings need you.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The talk
segments.narration: Then the talk, and keep it short. Three rules: pay only people you know, passwords stay in the app, and no job pays you first. And one promise: if something feels off, they can tell you, and nobody's in trouble. That promise matters most, because shame is what stops kids from telling anyone until it's too late.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Zoe's first paycheck summer
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up teen through one summer. Zoe is fifteen. By late June she has three hundred forty dollars in a payment app from babysitting and her birthday. Her feed knows it, or at least it feels that way. A post from an account with thousands of followers says: send fifty, get five hundred back in an hour, limited spots. The comments are full of people thanking the account.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a teenage girl on a bed scrolling a phone, a post with money emojis and many comments. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The flip, played out
segments.narration: Zoe's friend tried it last week, so here's how it went for him. He sent fifty. An hour later, a screenshot showed five hundred 'waiting' for him, but he had to pay a seventy-five dollar release fee first. He paid. Then came a 'tax'. He stopped at one hundred twenty-five dollars gone, and the account blocked him. The thank-you comments were other fake accounts. Nobody can multiply money you send them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone showing a fake balance screenshot, a teen boy looking upset. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The coin generator
segments.narration: In July, a video promises unlimited free coins for Zoe's favourite game, just log in on a website. Her younger brother almost does it. Zoe remembers the rule from the talk: passwords stay in the app. They look it up together and find people whose accounts were taken after using sites like it, with every skin and item gone, including ones bought with real money.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: two siblings looking at a game on a tablet, a login page with a red warning. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The babysitting job
segments.narration: In August, a family Zoe has never met texts to book her for a week of babysitting, and mails a check for six hundred eighty dollars, much more than the agreed two hundred. They ask her to send the extra to a 'furniture supplier' by payment app. Zoe tells her mom, which is the promise from the talk working. Her mom calls the bank, which explains a check can bounce days after the money shows up. They don't send anything, and the check bounces the next week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a mother and teen daughter at a kitchen table with a check and a phone, a bank call on speaker. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The scoreboard
segments.narration: The summer scoreboard: one money flip scrolled past, one game account kept, one fake check caught. Zero dollars lost. Zoe didn't need to know every scam. She needed three rules and someone she could tell without getting in trouble. If you're a parent, that last part is your job, and you can do it in one conversation this week.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a simple scoreboard with three green ticks, a teen and parent high-fiving. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If Zoe had sent the $50
segments.narration: And if Zoe had sent the fifty? The same day, she'd report the account inside the app, ask the payment app to dispute it, and stop replying, because the 'release fee' messages keep coming. She'd tell a parent, who can report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. The money is usually gone, but stopping at fifty instead of one twenty-five is still a win.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a teen showing a parent a phone, a report button highlighted. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If it happened
segments.narration: If it already happened, act the same day. Report the account inside the app. Change any password that was typed into a fake site. Call the bank about any check that was deposited. And report it at report fraud dot f t c dot gov. Then thank your teen for telling you.

script.title: Before Father's Day: car warranty calls, Google listing threats and the overpaying car buyer
script.hook: 3 scams go after dads who own a car or a small business. Here's each one, before Father's Day.

segments.heading: Why Dad
segments.narration: This one's for the dads, and everyone who has to explain things to one. If your dad owns a car or runs a small business, his phone probably rings with at least one of these every week. Three scams, what each one wants, and one simple answer for each.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Warranty calls
segments.narration: Scam one is the car warranty final notice. A robocall or an official-looking postcard says your warranty is about to expire. It's not from the carmaker or the dealer. Usually it's a seller of service contracts, which are not the same as a warranty, and some take a down payment and disappear. The FTC's advice is to hang up. Your dealer or the owner's manual tells you what you already have.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If he wants coverage
segments.narration: If Dad does want extra coverage, that's fine, but it's a decision for the kitchen table, not a cold call. Get the contract in writing. Read what's not covered, who does the repairs, and how to cancel. And compare it with simply saving the money for repairs.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Google listing calls
segments.narration: Scam two hits small business owners. A robocall says your business will be removed from Google today unless you press one. Then someone offers to fix it, or get you to the first page, for a fee. The FTC has taken action against robocallers using exactly this threat. A basic Google Business Profile is free, and you manage it yourself. Its cousin is the directory invoice, a bill for a listing nobody ordered. The FTC says don't pay invoices you can't match to an order.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The overpaying buyer
segments.narration: Scam three is for anyone selling a car, boat or trailer online. A buyer offers full price, doesn't need to see it, and sends a check for more than the price. Send the difference to my shipper, they say. The check bounces days later. The FTC warned car sellers about this one. The rule: never send back an overpayment, and get paid in a way you can confirm, like at your bank together.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Blocking calls
segments.narration: Now on screen, my own call log. Here's how to block a number, how to turn on your carrier's spam filter, and how to report a robocall at the FTC's site. It won't stop every call, but each report helps the FTC find the people behind them.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: For Father's Day
segments.narration: So for Father's Day, send him this, or better, sit down for ten minutes and set up his call filter together. One rule covers all three: hang up, and check it yourself with someone you already know, your dealer, your own business profile, your own bank.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Dad's week, made up
segments.narration: Let's run one made-up week for one dad. Tom is fifty-eight, drives a seven-year-old pickup, and runs a small landscaping business. Monday, a postcard says 'final notice' on his vehicle warranty. Wednesday, a robocall says his business will be removed from Google unless he presses one. Friday, a buyer offers full price for the trailer he listed online.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a man in work clothes at a pickup truck with a postcard, a phone and a trailer in the background. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The postcard
segments.narration: The postcard has his truck's make and year, which makes it feel real, but no carmaker logo and no dealer name. Tom calls the dealer where he bought the truck, using the number on his receipt. The dealer says the factory warranty expired years ago and that the card is from a seller of service contracts, which aren't the same thing. Tom recycles the card.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a postcard with bold urgent lettering being dropped in a recycling bin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The Google call
segments.narration: Wednesday's robocall says his business listing is about to be removed. Tom doesn't press one. He signs in to his own business profile, typed into the browser, and everything is there, unchanged. A basic listing is free to manage, and nobody needs to be paid to keep it. He reports the call at the FTC's site, so it gets added to the data the agency uses to go after robocallers.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a laptop showing a simple business listing with a green check, a phone with a call ended. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The trailer buyer
segments.narration: Friday, the trailer buyer doesn't want to see it, offers the full four thousand two hundred, and mails a cashier's check for five thousand nine hundred. 'Send the difference to my shipper.' Tom's daughter, the one who sent him this video, says it's the overpaying buyer from scam three. Tom takes the check to his own bank and asks them to verify it with the issuing bank. It's fake. If he'd wired the difference, he'd have lost seventeen hundred dollars and possibly the trailer.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a cashier's check under a magnifying glass at a bank counter, a trailer parked outside. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Setting up his phone
segments.narration: On Sunday, his daughter sits with him for ten minutes. They turn on the carrier's free spam filter, block the warranty number, and save the dealer's and the bank's numbers in his contacts so he can call them fast. That's the gift: not a lecture, ten minutes, and a dad who knows the one rule. Hang up, and check it yourself with someone you already know.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a father and adult daughter on a porch with a phone, coffee mugs, Sunday morning light. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: If he'd already paid
segments.narration: And if Tom had already bought one of those service contracts on a cold call? He'd read the contract for the cancellation terms, since many have a window for a refund, cancel in writing, and keep a copy. If he'd paid by card, he'd ask the card company about a dispute if the seller won't honour the terms. And he'd report the seller at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov.

script.title: Official-looking scams: jury duty warrants, deed letters and 'storage full' emails
script.hook: 3 scams borrow the look of something official: a court, a county office and your phone's own storage warning.

segments.heading: Borrowed authority
segments.narration: Some scams don't try to be your friend. They try to look official: a badge number, a seal, a case number, a deadline. That look does the work, because most of us don't argue with a court or a county office. Here are three of them, with the tells marked in pen.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jury duty
segments.narration: One, the jury duty warrant call. You missed jury duty, there's a warrant, pay the fine now to cancel it, with a payment app or gift cards. The federal courts have a page warning about this call. Courts send jury notices by mail, and they don't ask for your Social Security number or card by phone. Hang up and call the court yourself, using the number on its own website.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The deed letter
segments.narration: Two, the deed letter. Official seal, your parcel number, response due in ten days, get a certified copy of your deed for eighty-nine dollars. It's a private company, and the small print usually says so. The FTC says your county recorder can usually give you a copy for a few dollars, or free online. The same trick is used for homestead exemptions and property tax appeals, which you can usually file yourself.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Storage full
segments.narration: Three, the storage email. Your cloud storage is full, your photos will be deleted, upgrade now with a discount. The link goes to a lookalike page for your card details. Now my own phone: Settings, my name, storage. That's the real number, and it's one tap from the home screen.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: The pattern
segments.narration: Put the three side by side and the pattern is the same. Authority, a deadline, and a way to pay or click right now. Real courts, counties and phone companies give you time, and they let you check through their own website.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: One check
segments.narration: So here's the one check that works on all three. Don't use the phone number, the link, or the address in the message. Find the court, the county or the company yourself, and ask. If it's real, they'll tell you. If it isn't, you've lost nothing but five minutes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mrs. Alvarez's mail pile
segments.narration: Let's run the one check on a made-up week. Mrs. Alvarez is seventy-six. On Monday, a call says she missed jury duty and a warrant will be served tonight unless she pays a nine hundred dollar bond by payment app. On Wednesday, a letter with a gold seal and her parcel number says she should order a certified copy of her deed for eighty-nine dollars. On Friday, an email says her photos will be deleted because her storage is full.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: an older woman at a kitchen table with a phone, an official-looking letter and a tablet. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Monday: the court
segments.narration: Monday, the caller is calm and uses a real judge's name. Mrs. Alvarez says she'll call the court back, and the caller warns her not to hang up. She hangs up anyway. Her grandson looks up the county court's number on its own website and calls. The clerk says there's no warrant, the court doesn't take payments by phone, and jury notices come by mail.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a young man reading a court website on a laptop, his grandmother on a landline beside him. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Wednesday: the deed
segments.narration: Wednesday, they read the small print on the deed letter together. It's a private company, not the county. They look up the county recorder's office, typed in, and find she can get a copy of her deed there for a small fee, or view it online, and nothing is due in ten days. The letter goes in the shredder.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a letter with a gold seal going into a shredder, a laptop showing a county office page. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Friday: the storage email
segments.narration: Friday, she doesn't tap the email. Her grandson shows her where the real storage number lives, in her phone's own settings. She's using less than half. The email's link went to a lookalike page asking for her card. They mark it as junk and delete it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a phone settings screen showing a storage bar half full, an email moved to junk. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: What it added up to
segments.narration: Add up the week: nine hundred for the fake bond, eighty-nine for the deed copy, and a card number for the storage page. One check, three times: don't use their number, link or address. Find the court, the county or the company yourself, and ask. And notice who helped: a grandson who sits with the mail pile once a week. That habit is worth more than any single tip.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a calendar with three crossed-out scams and a small saved jar, a grandmother and grandson smiling. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why the look works
segments.narration: Why did any of this feel real? Look at what each one borrowed. The jury call borrowed a real judge's name, which is public. The deed letter borrowed her parcel number, which is in public property records. The storage email borrowed the look of her phone's own warnings. Real details make a fake message feel true, so a correct detail is not proof. Only checking through the real source is.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes: a magnifying glass over a seal, a case number and a clock, all marked as borrowed. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.narration: If Mrs. Alvarez had paid the bond by payment app, she'd call the app and her bank the same day and report it as fraud, then report it at ReportFraud dot FTC dot gov. If she'd paid for the deed copy, she could report the company to her state attorney general. And either way, the weekly mail pile check with her grandson keeps going.

script.hook: 3 scams pick up around the 4th of July. One goes after people whose pets ran from the fireworks.

segments.heading: The weekend
segments.narration: Long weekends are busy for scammers too. People are distracted, shopping, traveling, and on the 4th, a lot of pets bolt when the fireworks start. Here are three scams that pick up around the holiday, and a simple answer for each.

segments.heading: Lost pets
segments.narration: One, the lost pet text. You post a flyer with your number, and a text arrives: I think I found your dog, send me the code I'm about to text so I know you're the owner. The code is a sign-up code for an account in your name. The other version asks for gas money to bring the pet back. The Better Business Bureau has warned about both. A real finder sends a photo and meets you. No codes, and no money before you see your pet.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Before the 4th
segments.narration: Before the fireworks, check your pet's microchip details are current and the tag has your number. When you post a flyer, hold back one detail only you know, and ask callers to describe it. And call local shelters every day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Sent by mistake
segments.narration: Two, the accidental payment. Three hundred dollars arrives in your payment app from a stranger, then a polite message: so sorry, can you send it back? Their payment came from a stolen card or account, and it gets reversed. The three hundred you sent back from your own money doesn't. Venmo and Cash App both warn about this. Don't send it back. Contact support inside the app and let them reverse it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and cream with teal and amber warning accents, simple shapes. Face cam or screen recording; see original_element No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Biscuit runs off
segments.narration: Let's follow one made-up holiday weekend. On the Fourth at nine forty, the fireworks start and the Garcias' beagle, Biscuit, slips out the gate. They post a flyer on a neighborhood group with a photo and a phone number. Within twenty minutes, a text: 'I think I have your dog. I'm going to send you a code to make sure you're the owner, read it back to me.'

segments.heading: The code, and the real finder
segments.narration: Mrs. Garcia doesn't send the code. Instead she asks what the dog's left front paw looks like, the one detail she kept off the flyer. The texter goes quiet. The next morning a neighbor calls: Biscuit is in her garage. She describes the white sock on the left paw before Mrs. Garcia even asks. That's how you know.

segments.narration: Saturday, three hundred dollars lands in Mr. Garcia's payment app from a name he doesn't know, followed by a polite message asking him to send it back. He doesn't. He contacts the payment app through the app itself and reports it. Two days later, the payment is reversed, because it came from a stolen card. If he'd sent three hundred back, that money would have been his own.

segments.narration: One weekend, three traps, nothing lost, and the dog's asleep on the sofa. None of it needed expert knowledge: keep one detail of your pet off the flyer, never send back money you didn't ask for, and check any famous-face deal before you buy. Before the next long weekend, check your pet's microchip details and set your payment app to private.

segments.narration: And if Mrs. Garcia had read the code back? That code was likely a sign-up check for an account being opened with her phone number, often a messaging or calling account the scammer then uses for other scams in her name. She'd go to that service's site or app, typed in, and reclaim or report the account, and turn on two-step verification on her main accounts that day.

segments.narration: Here's the five-minute check the Garcias did the next week. They looked up Biscuit's microchip number on the registry their vet used and updated the phone number, which still had their old one. They added a tag with a current number. And they wrote down the one detail they'd keep off any future flyer. Small things, but on a fireworks night, they're what get a pet home fast.
